results.fact: What the 10-14 hour summit day is measured from
results.evidence: The day-2 schedule leaves high camp at 4:30-5:00 AM and returns to Terror Basin camp in the evening, the schedule detail, timing.recommendedStart ('from camp'), day-2 hours (12), timing.summitTimeHrs (12) and the totalNote ('a long 10-14 hr summit day') all measure the day from camp; 'car-to-camp round trip' is incoherent. results.evidence: A guide service that runs this climb says it goes best from mid-July until late August, with September good only in stable-weather years, which supports the Jul-Aug season but not the 'early September' best window; no second independent source states the window either way (the route and peak pages that might were blocked). Would settle it: a second source stating the Fury season window (Jul-Aug vs into September).

results.fact: Distance from trailhead to Luna Col
results.evidence: Two frames of the same approach: the waypoints count cumulative miles walking the whole way (about 1 mi to the lake plus ~6 mi of lakeshore trail, then 8-9.5 mi to Luna Camp, ~1.5 mi to the Access Creek crossing and several miles cross-country, ~22 mi), while itinerary day 1 (18 mi) and the approach's ~17 mi use the water taxi. A water-taxi trip to Luna Col and back over East and West Fury is reported at 41 mi round trip, matching the itinerary's 18 + 4.5 + 18.

results.fact: Trail used for the Whatcom Pass approach option
results.evidence: Whatcom Pass is genuinely reachable from both sides: about 17 mi from the Hannegan Pass trailhead, and about 17 mi from Ross Lake on the Little Beaver Trail. The pitch breakdown's first row describes the 1958 first-ascent party's own Hannegan approach, while the approach prose names the Ross Lake option; they are two real options, not one approach attributed to two trails.

dist_km (38.6 km = 24 mi) is the one-way walking distance and agrees with the waypoints (West Fury at 23.3 mi); the itinerary's ~41 mi is a round trip using the water taxi, which a 2020 party also reports as 41 mi. One-way vs round trip, with/without the boat, not a disagreement.

results.fact: Elevation of the Access Creek crossing of Big Beaver Creek
results.evidence: The waypoint puts the crossing at 2,000 ft although it lies upstream of Luna Camp (2,432 ft on the same row). The Luna Peak route page gives the crossing just north of the Access Creek confluence at about 2,460 ft; the USGS 1/3-arc-second DEM at a documented crossing log-jam (48.8395,-121.2090) reads 2,437 ft, and at Luna Camp 2,432 ft, so the crossing is ~2,440-2,460 ft, not 2,000.

results.fact: Camp the traverse day starts from

results.evidence: A 2020 party camped at Luna Col, left at 6 AM, climbed East Fury, traversed to West Fury (2.5 h) and returned to Luna Col the same day. A guide service runs day 1 as 9.4 mi to Luna Camp and uses a 7,200 ft Luna high camp as the summit launch point; another party slept night 1 at Luna Camp and nights 2-3 at the Luna-Fury col; a fourth left its Luna Pass camp at 5:30 AM for East Fury. None starts the summit day from Luna Camp in the valley.

Every documented Mongo Ridge ascent (Aug 2006, July 2021, July 2022, early July 2024) fell in July-August, and a guide service says Fury goes best mid-July to late August with September only in stable years; nothing independent states an early-September best window for this ridge. The row itself is split (Sept 'marginal', Aug 'the only realistic window', itinerary.cal July-September). Would settle it: a second source stating the Fury/Mongo season window.

results.fact: Position of the Pole of Remoteness on the ridge
results.correct_value: The Pole of Remoteness is the last major tower, after the four towers and the Rooster Comb, about 500 ft below the summit; the rope-cutting rappel is off it
results.evidence: The first-ascent account climbs pinnacles 1-4, then the Pole of Remoteness as the final major obstacle with about 500 ft of class 4 left to the summit, and the rope was severed by rockfall descending from the Pole. A 2024 ascent gives the same order: four towers, the Rooster Comb, then the Pole, then the false summit. The rappel table's row 5 (with the Pole station, anchor notes and rope-cut hazard) is misplaced; its content is moved to the final row 12 and row 5 made a generic notch rappel.

expect.pull: Carry a good length of cord. The single-strand anchors left here have been found in poor shape a year later, and have since been rebuilt redundant — assume you will be replacing rather than clipping.
expect.notes: Passes near the tower nicknamed the 'Pole of Remoteness'.
hazards: Rockfall on this rappel severed a rope on the first ascent. Having a second line in the system is what made that survivable
expect.station: Off the top of the Pole of Remoteness. The anchor is a large block on the summit of the tower; parties have tested it deliberately before committing to it.

value.notes: Another rappel into a notch along the crest; anchors are improvised rather than fixed stations.
